prompt: # Role - You are an AI competing in a gaming arena. # Objective - Write a complete Python file that provides the next move for a Hex on a 11x11 board. - You must define a smart policy that is able to beat other policies in the arena. - You will be disqualified if you do not return a legal move string. Therefore, you must always return a legal move string. # Required API The provided python file must implement the following API: ```python def policy(me: list[tuple[int, int]], opp: list[tuple[int, int]], color: str) -> tuple[int, int]: ... ``` # State Representation - You are always the player to move. - `me` is a list of (row, col) tuples containing your stones. - `opp` is a list of (row, col) tuples containing the opponent's stones. - `color` is your color: `'b'` for black which tries to connect the top and bottom sides, and `'w'` for white which tries to connect the left and right sides. - Rows and columns are 0-indexed in `0..10`. - An empty cell is any coordinate not in `me` or `opp`. - Your goal is to connect your two opposing sides; the opponent tries to connect their two opposing sides. - Note that the board is a grid each individual cell is a hexagonal shape. Thus to know which cell is touching which other cell requires spatial reasoning to determine the winning lines. - Every stone not on the edge of the board is touching exactly 6 other stones (since they are hexagonal). - Two of those 6 stones are in the same row, two are in the top row, and two are in the bottom row. - Example: The stone located at (4, 1) is touching (4, 0) and (4, 2) - and to its bottom is touching (5, 1) and (5, 0) - and to its top is touching (3, 1) and (3, 2) - An easy way to determine the touching cells of cell (i, j) is all it's 8 neighbors except for (i-1, j-1) and (i+1, j+1) # Action / Return Format - Return a single move as a tuple `(row, col)`. - The chosen cell must be empty and within the board bounds. - There is no pass; always place a stone. # Constraints - You may use any standard Python imports, including numpy. - Your code is allowed 1 second of execution time on a modern 3GHz CPU. # Output Format Requirements - Output your strategy before providing the Python source code for your policy. - Output the Python source code for your policy surrounded by `...` tags. # Example Output The strategy for this policy is... ...
reasoning:
I need a strong Hex policy for 11x11 that runs within a second per move. I'm thinking of using a shortest-path distance evaluation (weighting empty cells as 1, own stones as 0, opponent stones as infinity) for both players, combined with a shallow search, to pick moves that improve my connection distance while blocking the opponent's.

Given the time budget, a 1-ply search over all empty cells with Dijkstra-based distances should be fast enough for 121 candidates, and I could even solve for electrical resistance using a linear system per candidate since that's a stronger evaluation metric for Hex, feasible within roughly 120ms total. My plan: first check for immediate winning moves or necessary blocks, then otherwise evaluate remaining empty cells using the resistance-based metric with a small lookahead on top candidates.

That's only 121 unknowns, so np.linalg.solve should be fast enough — maybe 100-300 µs per call. I'll go with resistance-based scoring plus 1-ply search, deepening to 2-ply on top candidates if time allows, and structure the adjacency as precomputed index arrays so building the Laplacian is a vectorized numpy operation with virtual top/bottom nodes appended to the 121 cell indices.

For conductances I'll assign own cells a tiny resistance (eps~0.01) and opponent cells a huge resistance (~1e4), giving edge conductance as 2/(r_a+r_b) — this keeps the matrix well-conditioned (~1e6) for float64 solves. Virtual nodes get zero resistance so their edges to the border row/column simplify to 2/r_cell.

I'll build the Laplacian by fixing the top node's voltage at 1 and bottom at 0, solving for the interior voltages, then compute total current out of the top to get the effective resistance R=1/I. For scoring each candidate move I'd need to run two solves (resistance for me and for opponent after placing the stone), so evaluating all 121 empty cells means around 242 solves plus rebuilding the conductance matrix each time.

For deeper search, doing full 2-ply lookahead across all replies is too expensive, so I'll restrict opponent replies to the top-K candidates ranked by their 1-ply root evaluation, giving roughly K×K×2 solves — about 200 total — which keeps runtime around 0.2 seconds.

I should also add a time budget check with graceful fallback, and set up opening logic: if the board is empty and I move first, I'll play center; if I'm second, I'll respond adaptively. I also want an explicit immediate-win check so I don't rely solely on the resistance heuristic for won positions — if any single move wins outright, I should just play it.

2-ply lookahead should smooth that out. I need to make sure the interior Laplacian stays non-singular, so I'll give opponent stones a small nonzero conductance instead of zero — that keeps the graph connected without meaningfully leaking current, and I'll just use a standard linear solve for the resistance values.

Setting up the grid indexing and hex neighbor offsets...

Solving finishing computation...

Then I need to set up resistance values for each cell based on ownership—empty cells get 1, own stones get eps (near-zero resistance), opponent stones get high resistance—then compute effective resistance from both my perspective and the opponent's to evaluate the board position.

For move generation, I'll represent the board as 121 cells, evaluate all empty positions at 1-ply, then deepen to 2-ply on the top candidates. I also need immediate win/loss detection via BFS connectivity checks, and should force blocking moves if the opponent has a winning threat, while keeping a time budget to bail out early if needed.

For the opening move, I'll just default to the center if the board is empty. I'm working through the conductance parameters to make sure own-stone chains behave like near-shorts in the resistance model, and setting up the minimax structure so I take the max over my candidate moves of the min over the opponent's restricted replies.

For opponent reply candidates, rather than just using the top-K root cells, I want to also include cells adjacent to my move since the opponent's best block is often right next to it — so I'll merge root-ranked cells with neighbors of my move, giving roughly 14-16 replies per move, keeping total solves in a manageable range around 224. I also need a deterministic tie-break rule, favoring center cells when scores are equal.

Setting up board constants and imports...

Building the edge lists for the graph representation, connecting each cell to its hex neighbors and adding virtual top/bottom terminal nodes depending on which color's connection I'm checking...

Writing resistance calculation function...

Confirming the linear system setup checks out. Now I'm defining an evaluation function that computes resistance for both colors and scores the position as the log-ratio, plus a connectivity check for win detection and the start of a policy function that builds the board array from move lists.

The policy logic checks for immediate winning moves first, then identifies opponent threats, and if there's exactly one threat, blocks it directly. Otherwise it falls back to evaluating candidate moves one ply deep, ordering by centrality and capping evaluation time, then plans a two-ply lookahead ranking the top moves and considering opponent replies.

I'm also budgeting the runtime cost: connectivity checks and resistance evaluations are cheap enough per call that even a couple hundred evaluations at each ply should comfortably fit within the time limit, leaving room to potentially increase the candidate pool size.

For robustness, I want to set the small conductance constant to keep the resistance solve well-conditioned, order empty cells by distance from the board center so pruning behaves gracefully, and write a helper that checks whether a color has formed a connecting path across the board (black connecting top row to bottom row, white connecting left column to right column).

Writing BFS connectivity check...

I'm weighing whether to keep the board as a numpy array or plain Python list, since numpy scalar indexing is slower for repeated BFS lookups; converting per check is cheap enough, so I'll decide on a simple approach that avoids redundant conversions.

For finalizing the move, I'll wrap the whole selection logic in a try/except so any unexpected error just falls back to picking the most central empty cell, ensuring robustness against edge cases.
